newsitem.title: BOSNIA: U.S., Europe differ over Bosnia aid conference.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Europe differ over Bosnia aid conference.

text.p: The United States and European envoys are arguing about how to respond to a refusal by Bosnian Serb leaders to approve economic laws needed to raise reconstruction aid, diplomats said on Thursday.
Washington has pushed for postponement of an international fund-raising conference for Bosnia on June 24 after the country's Serb entity dropped its support for a package of economic laws.
Major powers set adoption of the economic legislation, including a customs and tariffs law, as a precondition for the conference in Brussels.

But European governments wanted to hold the conference for the country's Moslem-Croat federation -- which has accepted the economic laws -- and freeze aid to the Serb territory until the laws were adopted.
"We've been under severe pressure from the U.S. government for quite some time to postpone the conference," Carl Bildt, the outgoing international High Representative to Bosnia, told reporters.
"To postpone, when we still have a chance of meeting the conditions by using pressure, is to make virtually certain that the conditions will not be met," Bildt said in a farewell news conference.

Bildt, who is being succeeded by former Spanish U.N. ambassador Carlos Westendorp, said the disagreement over tactics illustrated the need for the international community to present a united front in Bosnia.
"This is rather a good example for working together with a coordinated approach," he said.

Diplomats said Washington wanted to stick to warnings delivered by major powers last month that the aid conference would go ahead only after the adoption of laws on a central bank, budget, service of foreign debt and customs rates.
Bildt, whose aides complained that he was often undermined by the Americans during his 18-month tenure, delivered veiled criticism of Washington at his news conference.
Bildt said a renewed commitment by the United States to enforce terms of the Dayton peace treaty was welcome but he hinted that the Americans sometimes had a "short-term" approach.
"Peace making is not a question of quick fixes, one-liners and photo opportunites. Peace making is the result of persistence and patience of those working on the ground...," he said.
Westendorp, who formally took over his post on Thursday, praised his predecessor and said he faced a "huge task" in ensuring the Dayton accords were carried out in full.
The deputy to the High Representative, German envoy Michael Steiner, is also stepping down after serving for 18 months.
Westendorp said he expected to appoint two deputies, an American yet to be named and Gerd Wagner, a German diplomat who currently serves in Washington.
